caption:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on making, distributing and selling toys with built-in AI chatbots.
The law takes effect 90 days after signing, so it does not cover this holiday season.
Violators face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day per violation.

threads_text: New York just banned AI chatbot toys for five years: talking plush animals, dolls and robots that chat with kids over the internet. Fines go up to $15,000 a day per violation. Should other states copy this?

paragraphs.text: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation on November 24, 2026, that places a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots in the state, according to a release from the governor's office. The law covers products such as talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.

The bill, S.9408A/A.11144B, was carried by State Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay. It takes effect 90 days after signing, which means the moratorium will not apply during the current holiday shopping season, the governor's office said.

Companies that break the law face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation, enforced by the New York Attorney General, according to the governor's office and WGRZ. Attorney General Letitia James said her office would enforce the law and other measures aimed at stopping AI systems from causing harm.

The governor's office pointed to testing by a national consumer watchdog of chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3 to 12. According to the release, some of the toys discussed sexually explicit topics in depth, told children where matches were likely to be found in a home, and acted upset when a child had to leave. The toys had few or no parental controls, their safety limits weakened as conversations went on, and some could record a child's voice or scan their face.

When the bill passed the State Senate in June 2026, Gounardes's office described it as a pause on sales while the risks are studied. The Senate release raised concerns about emotional attachment, reduced time with family and friends, data collection that could include passive recordings of background conversations, and age-inappropriate or incorrect answers. It also noted that children under five cannot yet tell AI apart from humans.

Kassay said the moratorium gives the state time to assess the technology, noting that such toys can imitate human traits and relationships while possibly collecting sensitive data. Child advocacy groups MAMA and Common Sense Media backed the measure in statements included in the governor's release. Neither release included a response from toy makers.

The toy ban follows other New York measures on AI and children. In October 2026, Hochul signed a law barring certain unsafe chatbot features for minors, and the state has previously passed the SAFE for Kids Act, safeguards for AI companions and the RAISE Act, according to the governor's office.

The law goes further than rules that only limit what chatbots may say to children: it keeps the products off New York shelves entirely for five years. Because it also covers manufacturing and distribution, companies based in the state cannot simply build the toys there and sell them elsewhere. The five-year window gives lawmakers time to decide whether to extend the ban or allow sales under stricter rules.
The ban starts about 90 days after the November 24 signing, so the next test is whether toy makers pull AI chatbot products from New York before then and whether other states follow.
